newsitem.title: INDIA: Death hovers in the air on Indian capital's roads.
newsitem.headline: Death hovers in the air on Indian capital's roads.

text.p: Mounting pollution in the Indian capital has claimed nearly 7,500 lives in the past year and caused deformed and premature babies to be born to its residents, officials and analysts said on Monday.
"About 7,500 people died premature deaths and 2.5 million were treated for various pollution-related diseases in the city in 1996," Delhi's Transport Minister Rajendra Gupta said.
"The mounting pollution level in the city is affecting newborns as well and is leading to the birth of premature and even deformed babies," Gupta told Reuters by telephone.

The Indian capital is the world's fourth most polluted city. About three-fourths of New Delhi's total atmospheric pollution is caused by vehicular emissions -- about 900 tonnes a day, or one-third the amount in India's 12 largest cities put together.
Environmental analysts say an overdose of pollution adversely affects foetuses and hampers children's mental growth.

Suspended particulate matter, a barometer of the air pollution, was five times higher in New Delhi than levels permitted by the Indian government, said Anju Sharma, an expert at the independent Centre for Science and Environment (CSE).
Delhi's roads are clogged with nearly 2.8 million vehicles every day and another 150,000 to 200,000 are added every year, an official at the Central Road Research Institute (CRRI) told Reuters.

The city accounts for nearly 10 percent of India's automobile population. "Every tenth vehicle in India is registered in Delhi," said T.S. Reddy, head of the traffic and transportation division at CRRI.
Reddy said the city needed to develop an effective public transport system.
"To bring down the number of vehicles on the road the government has to provide the citizens with a good mass transport system," Reddy said.

Delhi, with a population of nearly 11 million, is the only major city of the world served by only bus transport. A small and infrequent suburban train service provides poor back-up. There are no trams.
"Delhi really lacks an adequate public transport system. Once we have a good public transport system, a lot of our problems would be solved," CSE's Sharma said.
Analysts said the government was not doing enough to curb pollution and most measures were cosmetic.
"It is all an eyewash as things like catalytic converters are no solution to the actual problem of pollution in the city," said Sharma.

In 1995, India stepped up its battle against pollution by making it mandatory for new cars to use lead-free fuel and ordered car manufacturers to fit vehicles with catalytic converters to neutralise harmful emissions.
"The pollution standards were heavily watered down due to lobbying by automobile manufacturers," Sharma said.
High fuel costs were forcing the government to compromise on the quantity for the sake of quality, Sharma said.
"We are importing inferior crude oil from abroad and our refineries do not have the requisite equipment to deal with the high sulphur content in the crude," she said.
"Due to the duty (tax) benefits on diesel we are producing more quantities of diesel and are compromising on its quality," she added. "I think we are heading for a disaster."
